paragraphs.text: Good evening, elders and sisters. Hopefully you're having a great day. I had a great day today. Got up and visited some missionaries in Malolos and Tabang and Baliuag. By the way, those of you who we visited today all look great. It was so wonderful to see you. Sister Hughes and I enjoyed that part of our day immensely. We don't have any updates for you today, but we are excited to share—I'm excited to share these thoughts from the conclusion of the second chapter of Drawing on the Powers of Heaven. It starts with this title, Faith: The Key to Excellence. That's an interesting title, that faith would be the key to excellence. We might think, well, diligence is, or knowledge is, or education is, but what the author is putting forth is that faith is the key to excellence.

Excuse me, now he says this in support of that idea. In the course of your life, there are many things required of you that you cannot accomplish to the degree of excellence without the Lord's help. There will be many things that you will do every day that you could do much better if you knew how to call down the powers of heaven to assist you. In order to realize your full potential, you must learn how to exercise such faith in the process of drawing down the power of heaven that the Lord will actually help you achieve your righteous desires.

Now those desires could be very secular. They could be getting a good education. They could be getting a good job. They could be getting a better pay for your work that you're doing. All kinds of things that go on in our lives, we should be able to draw on the powers of heaven to help us get those things, to help us live a higher quality life. Exercising such faith involves a very specific process, which we've said before, and it has to be learned, and not just learned, it has to be mastered.

Now it starts with righteousness. Unless your life is in harmony with the basic principles and tenets of the gospel—for example, purity of thought, actions, proper motives, obedience, dedication, so forth—you will not be able to exercise sufficient faith to actually release the powers of heaven. The Lord has stipulated that the powers of heaven cannot be controlled nor handled only upon the principles of righteousness. When you are keeping the Lord's commandments, when you're doing your church callings conscientiously, when you're refraining from inappropriate conversations, you are putting yourself into the position where you can actually pull down the powers of heaven to bless your life.

The Lord says in D&C 82 verse 10: "I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise." Elder Bruce R. McConkie of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles tells us that, quote, "Faith is a gift of God bestowed as a reward for personal righteousness. It is always given when righteousness is present, and the greater the measure of obedience to God's laws, the greater will be the endowment of faith," close quote. Consequently, faith as a principle of power can only be exercised by those people who conform to the principles of the truth that come from God.

Now, moving away from that, let's talk about righteous desires and faith. The Lord's promise that He will grant unto men according to their desires. In Alma 29 verse 4, we read: "...I know that he granteth unto men according to their desire..." "Verily, verily, I say unto you, even as you desire of me so it shall be done unto you," and that comes from Doctrine and Covenants section 11 verse 8.

Desire, however, elders and sisters, is more than just wishing for something. It's actually a motivating conviction that moves a person to action. For instance, Alma—Alma's strong desire to see the people join the Church is very evident when he goes on his mission to the people in the city of Ammonihah. They reject his message pretty aggressively, I might add. When Alma first attempted to preach to the people, they literally threw him out of the city. But Alma still desired to see them baptized. He prayed that the Lord would prepare a way so that he could baptize them. And the record says that he, quote, "labored much in the spirit, wrestling with God in mighty prayer, that he would pour out his Spirit upon the people who were in the city, that he would also grant that he," Alma, "might baptize them unto repentance." You can find that in Alma chapter 8 verse 10.

Then according to Alma's desire, the Lord prepared the way for him to convert one very prominent man in the city of Ammonihah. His name was Amulek. You remember the story, also in chapter 8. Following his conversion, Amulek joins Alma in the ministry. As a result of their teaching, a few people in Ammonihah begin to repent and to search the scriptures. Amulek continues to assist Alma in the ministry over the next several years and the establishment of the Church becomes general, in other words successful, throughout the land in all the region roundabout among all the people of the Nephites. From Alma's account of the missionary labors, it's obvious that Amulek played a huge role in the establishment of the Church. It appears that Alma's ultimate success in seeing thousands baptized would never have been realized if he had not desired with all his heart to baptize the people in Ammonihah even after they had rejected his message.

Later, when Alma decides to go on a mission to the Zoramites, he again prays for success. We have a record of the prayer. He says, quote, "O Lord, wilt thou comfort my soul, and give unto me success... O Lord, wilt thou grant unto us that we may have success in bringing them," the people of the Zoramites, "again unto thee in Christ." You'll find that in Alma 31 verse 32 and 34. Once again, Alma's convinced the Lord that he's willing to pay any price to succeed in his missionary labors. Alma goes on to say, "O Lord, wilt thou give me strength, that I may bear with mine infirmities... O Lord, wilt thou grant unto me that I may have strength, that I may suffer with patience these afflictions which shall come upon me." Again, that's Alma 31. Again, the Lord granted according to his desires and gave him success in his labors.

Do you see this pattern? As we look at the pattern, we see it repeat itself in different missionaries throughout the Book of Mormon and the Bible. Look at Ammon as an example. Ammon's desire resulted in the conversion of a very influential man, King Lamoni. The way it was then opened and thousands were baptized. It's important to realize that Ammon was not successful in his missionary labors until his desires had motivated him to be patient and long-suffering in his afflictions. He had experienced many afflictions. He had suffered much, both in body and mind, with hunger, thirst, and fatigue, just as Alma had. So did Ammon labor in the spirit. You'll find that in Alma 17:5. In other words, he had to convince the Lord that he wanted to baptize the Lamanites and was willing to pay any price in order to succeed. Then the Lord granted unto him according to his prayers and desires.

Modern-day missionaries like us will be much more successful in their labors if we will heed Elder McConkie's counsel: "Perhaps what is wrong is that we have not desired in faith with all our hearts to bring souls into the kingdom. Perhaps we have not made up our minds that we can bring people into the Church." If the missionaries cultivate a sincere desire to baptize people and convince the Lord they're willing to pay any price in terms of hard work, etc., the Lord will grant their desires and they will be instruments in baptizing converts.

What Elder McConkie says regarding desire in the context of missionary work applies to all your righteous desires. If you're not realizing your righteous desires, the truth is you're not desiring them with sufficient faith, or in other words, with all your heart. If you don't do that, the Lord can't assist you in realizing your righteous desires. Remember, you'll receive according to your desires, but these desires are desires that are deep, convicting motivations, like Alma's, like Ammon's. Elder McConkie goes on to say, quote, "If we desire to get such and such a thing and have faith in the Lord, it is going to happen," close quote.

If you set a goal to achieve a particular righteous desire and then you find you lack initiative in pursuing the goal, you must conclude the goal is not really a true desire. If it were a true desire, you would be motivated to action. Many people will say, 'Oh, well, I'd give up anything if I could just play the piano like that,' when in reality, they would never pay the price of practicing every day for years to perfect the talent of playing the piano like a true, you know, a true gifted, talented piano player. If you truly desire something, you will have the necessary motivation to pursue the goal completely. By contrast, if your goal is not a sincere desire, you're just not going to be able to summon up the motivation to get after it when things get a little tough.

Attitudes and desires are formed as a direct result of what we think about. I want you to get this, elders and sisters. This is very important. I'm going to repeat that. Attitudes and desires are formed as a direct result of what we think about. When a person chooses not to use his free will in directing his thoughts, he leaves the dimensions of the mind that control his desires wide open to suggestion. And that suggestion can come from places that don't have your best interest at heart. If we do not make an extended effort to control and direct our thinking, our desires and attitudes will be influenced primarily by the adversary, by other people, music, movies, TV, radio, and so forth. So you have the choice of deliberately directing your own thinking or allowing other forces to decide your desires and attitudes.

But make no mistake, elders and sisters, we are responsible for our thoughts. Consequently, as individuals, we are responsible for our attitudes and desires because our thoughts govern our inner desires. We are ambitious or lazy, interesting or dull, faithful or disobedient, dependable or undependable, successful or unsuccessful, according to our attitudes and desires. And frankly, whether we realize many righteous desires or few is dependent in large measure on our frame of mind. Therefore, it is critically important that we learn to control our thoughts and focus on righteous desires.

So that concludes chapter two, and we start digging now, starting with chapter three, into very specific elements of this process. But before we finish tonight, let me just give you a few questions for you to think about. Number one, what is desire? Write an answer to that. Hopefully you've captured it in what I've read to you or said to you tonight. According to Elder McConkie, what must missionaries do in order to have more success in bringing people into the Church? And then finally, explain how a lack of desire and faith account for failure in other aspects of life. In other words, that question is, how can not having enough desire, not having enough faith, actually result in failure in other aspects of your life? Getting the education you want, getting the kind of job you want, getting the kind of spouse you want, having the kind of family you want, living in the kind of home you want, and so forth.

We must understand, and this is really important, Elder he says, we've got to understand, the Lord loves us. He wants to give us all of the good things. He says the earth is full and there's enough and to spare. He wants to give these things to us, but we have to follow the process. We have to have sufficient desire. We have to exercise faith to action. We have to exercise faith to power. And as we do those things, we literally draw to us the power from God to actually enlarge our capacity, our intellect, our talents, our gifts, such that we can reach out into the world and pull into our lives all these good things that the Lord desires to have us have. So that's it for today. I hope that it's been useful for you, and we'll take up chapter three, which is entitled, The Principles That Govern Faith, tomorrow. Good night. Love you.
